title: Cosmas and Damian (26 September)
hookLine: two doctors, remembered for healing without a fee, whose names are said at Mass

cards: Before you see a doctor these days, there's usually a form: insurance, payment, a signature at the bottom. Now strike all of that. A clinic with no front desk and no bill.

You walk in sick, you're treated, you walk out, and nobody asks for anything. That's the story the Church tells about two brothers who practiced medicine long ago. Their names are still spoken in a prayer of the Mass.

teach.h: TWO BROTHERS WHO HEALED WITHOUT PAY.
teach.b: Here's the story as tradition tells it. Cosmas and Damian were brothers, twins in some tellings, who trained as physicians somewhere in the eastern part of the Roman world.
They were Christians, and they treated the sick without taking payment.
The Eastern churches gave them a title for it, a Greek word that means, roughly, the ones without silver. During a persecution, the story goes, they were arrested and put to death for their faith.
Historians can say very little for certain about their lives; what is sure is that the Church kept their names. Why work for free?
Their story points straight to a line Jesus gave the apostles when he sent them out to heal.

teach.h: FREELY HAVE YOU RECEIVED, FREELY GIVE.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "Freely have you received, freely give." Healing, in that line, isn't a product. It's a gift passed along.

At a Mass where the priest uses the first Eucharistic Prayer, the old Roman Canon, listen for a list of names: Mary, Joseph, the apostles, then a run of early popes and martyrs, the same list that names Cornelius and Cyprian.
At the end of that list come two doctors: Cosmas and Damian.
When the priest prays that list in full, as the Missal allows him to shorten it, these brothers are named in the middle of the Mass.
Some doctors and pharmacists claim them as patrons, and some hospitals carry their names.
Their feast puts two ideas side by side: a healer's skill is a gift, and people who care for the sick are worth remembering by name.

how: Saints Cosmas and Damian are remembered on 26 September, and their names are said in the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I) whenever a priest uses it with its full list of saints; some Catholic doctors and hospitals keep their feast.

games.why: tradition says Cosmas and Damian treated the sick without payment, which is how they earned their title.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has cared for your body, a doctor, a nurse, a pharmacist, a parent who sat up with you through a fever, and remember one specific moment of their care.
If you pray, name them before God, the way the Mass names Cosmas and Damian; if you don't, just hold them in mind with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Without silver, the old title for healers like Cosmas and Damian, brothers and doctors who, tradition says, healed without charging, and whose names are still spoken in the Roman Canon.

orig.note: the Greek title the Eastern churches give healer saints like Cosmas and Damian: the ones without silver.

carryVoice: Your line: the free doctors. Healing as a gift, passed along from hand to hand. See you tomorrow.
